2015A16.goal: Two symmetric equations link $x$ and $y$, with $x\ne y$. We want $x^2+y^2$ without solving for $x$ and $y$. Subtracting the equations gives $x+y$; adding them brings in $x^2+y^2$.

tools.name: Dividing by $x-y$
tools.why: That is why the condition $x\ne y$ is given.

2015A16.approach: Subtract the second equation from the first: the left side gives $y-x$ and the right side factors with $x-y$. Cancel to get $x+y$. Then add the equations and expand to reach $x^2+y^2$.
2015A16.bridge: Subtract to get $x+y$, add to get $x^2+y^2$.
2015A16.shortcut: For symmetric systems, subtracting kills the symmetric part and adding keeps it.
2015A16.recognize: Symmetric pairs of equations with $x\ne y$: subtract and factor out $x-y$.

2015A17.goal: A line through the origin, the vertical line $x=1$, and the line $y=1+\tfrac{\sqrt3}3x$ form an equilateral triangle. We want its perimeter. Angles decide which line through the origin works.
2015A17.approach: The given lines meet at $60^\circ$ ($90^\circ-30^\circ$). The third line must make $60^\circ$ with both: direction $150^\circ$, i.e. $y=-\tfrac{\sqrt3}3x$. Then one side lies on $x=1$ and its length is easy.

steps.title: Find the third line
steps.explain: Directions $90^\circ$ and $30^\circ$. A direction making $60^\circ$ with both is $150^\circ$: slope $\tan150^\circ=-\tfrac{\sqrt3}3$. It passes through the origin: $y=-\tfrac{\sqrt3}3x$.

steps.title: Side on $x=1$
steps.explain: At $x=1$ the lines give $y=1+\tfrac{\sqrt3}3$ and $y=-\tfrac{\sqrt3}3$. The side length is $1+\tfrac{2\sqrt3}3$.

2015A17.bridge: Find the third line by angles, then measure the side on $x=1$.
solution: The given lines have directions $90^\circ$ and $30^\circ$; the third must be at $150^\circ$: $y=-\tfrac{\sqrt3}3x$.
On $x=1$ the triangle's side runs from $-\tfrac{\sqrt3}3$ to $1+\tfrac{\sqrt3}3$: length $1+\tfrac{2\sqrt3}3$.
2015A17.shortcut: A vertical side makes the length a simple difference of $y$-values.
traps: Choosing $y=\sqrt3x$ (direction $60^\circ$): it makes only $30^\circ$ with each given line, so the triangle is not equilateral.
Measuring a slanted side with only $y$-differences.
2015A17.recognize: Lines forming an equilateral triangle: think in directions; each pair must differ by $60^\circ$ (mod $180^\circ$).

2015A18.goal: Among $1$ to $1000$, count numbers whose base-$16$ form uses only the digits $0$–$9$. Convert $1000$ to hex to see how many hex digits we need.

tools.name: Counting digit strings
tools.why: $399_{16}=921<1000$, so every such string is in range.

2015A18.approach: $1000=3E8_{16}$, so numbers up to $1000$ have at most three hex digits with leading digit at most $3$. Any string $h_2h_1h_0$ with $h_2\in\{0..3\}$ and $h_1,h_0\in\{0..9\}$ is at most $399_{16}=921$, so all are in range. Count and remove zero.
2015A18.bridge: Convert $1000$ to hex and count strings with digits $0$–$9$.
solution: Valid numbers are $h_2h_1h_0$ with $h_2\le3$, $h_1,h_0\le9$, all at most $399_{16}=921<1000$.
Digit sum of $399$ is $21$. The answer is $\textbf{(E)}\ 21$.
2015A18.shortcut: Check the largest candidate ($399_{16}$) is below $1000$, so no partial counting is needed.
traps: Counting up to $3E8_{16}$ with letter digits.
2015A18.recognize: "Only certain digits in base $b$": convert the bound to base $b$ and count digit strings.

2015A19.goal: An isosceles right triangle with area $12.5$ has its right angle trisected; the trisectors meet the hypotenuse at $D$ and $E$. We want $[CDE]$. Coordinates make each trisector a simple line.

tools.name: Trisector lines
tools.why: Rays at $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$ from the right angle.

2015A19.approach: Put $C$ at the origin with legs on the axes, hypotenuse $x+y=5$. Find $D$ on the $30^\circ$ ray; $E$ is its mirror image in $y=x$. Then $[CDE]=\tfrac12|x_Dy_E-x_Ey_D|$.

check.q: On the line $x+y=5$, where does $y=x$ hit?
For $C$ at the origin, $D=(p,q)$, $E=(q,p)$, what is $[CDE]$?

2015A19.bridge: Coordinates with the hypotenuse $x+y=5$; intersect the $30^\circ$ ray and use symmetry.
solution: Legs $5$; hypotenuse $x+y=5$ with $C$ at the origin.
$D$ is on $y=\tfrac{x}{\sqrt3}$: $x_D=\tfrac{5\sqrt3}{\sqrt3+1}$; $E$ is the mirror image.
2015A19.recognize: Angle trisectors from a right angle: rays at $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$; coordinates turn them into lines.

2015A20.goal: For a rectangle with integer sides $l,w$, which listed value cannot be $A+P=lw+2l+2w$? Adding $4$ makes it factor.
2015A20.approach: $A+P+4=(l+2)(w+2)$, a product of two integers each at least $3$. Check which choice $+4$ cannot be written that way.

steps.title: Test the choices
steps.explain: $104=8\cdot13$, $106=2\cdot53$, $108=4\cdot27$, $110=10\cdot11$, $112=4\cdot28$. Only $106$ has no factorisation into two factors both $\ge3$ ($53$ is prime). So $A+P=102$ is impossible.

check.q: Can $106$ be written as a product of two integers both at least $3$?

2015A20.shortcut: Look for the choice where (choice $+4$) is $2\times$ prime.
2015A20.recognize: Expressions like $xy+ax+by$: add $ab$ to factor (Simon's trick), then reason about factor pairs.

2015A21.goal: Tetrahedron $ABCD$ has two faces that are $3$-$4$-$5$ right triangles sharing the hypotenuse $AB$, and a given $CD$. We want the volume. The key is that the two altitudes to $AB$ meet at the same point and are perpendicular.

tools.name: Altitude to the hypotenuse
tools.why: Area two ways, and the leg squared equals hypotenuse times adjacent segment.

2015A21.approach: Both $ABC$ and $ABD$ are right triangles with legs $3,4$ on hypotenuse $AB=5$, so the feet of their altitudes to $AB$ coincide at $H$. With $CH=DH=\tfrac{12}5$ and $CD=\tfrac{12}5\sqrt2$, angle $CHD=90^\circ$. Then $CH$ is perpendicular to the whole plane $ABD$ and is the height.

steps.title: Same foot
steps.explain: In $ABC$ (right at $C$), the foot $H$ of the altitude from $C$ is $\tfrac{AC^2}{AB}=\tfrac95$ from $A$. In $ABD$ (right at $D$, $AD=3$), the foot is also $\tfrac95$ from $A$. So both altitudes meet $AB$ at $H$, each of length $\tfrac{12}5$.

check.q: In a right triangle with legs $6,8$, how far from the end of leg $6$ is the altitude's foot on the hypotenuse?

steps.title: Perpendicular altitudes
steps.explain: $CH^2+DH^2=2\cdot\tfrac{144}{25}=\tfrac{288}{25}=CD^2$, so $\angle CHD=90^\circ$. $CH\perp AB$ and $CH\perp HD$, so $CH$ is perpendicular to plane $ABD$.

2015A21.bridge: Show the two altitudes to $AB$ share a foot and are perpendicular; use one as the height.
solution: $ABC$ and $ABD$ are $3$-$4$-$5$ right triangles on hypotenuse $AB$; their altitudes to $AB$ both have length $\tfrac{12}5$ and foot $H$ at $\tfrac95$ from $A$.
$CH^2+DH^2=CD^2$, so $CH\perp DH$; with $CH\perp AB$, $CH$ is perpendicular to plane $ABD$.
2015A21.shortcut: The given $CD=\tfrac{12}5\sqrt2$ is exactly $\sqrt2$ times the altitude: a hint that the two altitudes are perpendicular.
traps: Assuming the faces are perpendicular without checking.
2015A21.recognize: Tetrahedra built from known triangles: look for a point where two altitudes meet at a right angle; that altitude is the height.

2015A22.goal: Eight people around a table flip coins; we want the probability no two neighbours both get heads. Count circular arrangements of $8$ bits with no two adjacent $1$s, then divide by $2^8$.

tools.name: Linear count (Fibonacci)
tools.why: Condition on the first bit: $0$ then any valid $n-1$ string, or $10$ then any valid $n-2$ string.

tools.name: Breaking the circle
tools.why: If person $1$ sits, the rest form a line; if person $1$ stands, both neighbours sit.

2015A22.approach: Fix person $1$. If tails, persons $2$–$8$ form a line of $7$ with no adjacent heads. If heads, persons $2$ and $8$ must be tails, and persons $3$–$7$ form a free line of $5$. Use the Fibonacci counts.

steps.title: Linear counts
steps.explain: Lines of length $1,2,3,\ldots$ have $2,3,5,8,13,21,34$ valid strings. So length $5$: $13$; length $7$: $34$.

check.q: How many length-$4$ strings have no two adjacent $1$s?

steps.title: Circle
steps.explain: Person $1$ tails: $34$. Person $1$ heads: $13$. Total $47$. Probability $\tfrac{47}{256}$.

2015A22.bridge: Case on person $1$ and use Fibonacci counts for the remaining lines.
solution: Person $1$ seated: the other $7$ form a line: $34$ ways.
Person $1$ standing: persons $2$ and $8$ sit; persons $3$–$7$ form a line: $13$ ways.
2015A22.shortcut: The circular count is the Lucas number $L_8=47$.
traps: Using the linear count $F_{10}=55$ (forgets the circle).
Forgetting the case where person $1$ stands.
2015A22.recognize: "No two adjacent" on a circle: break the circle by casework on one position, then use the linear Fibonacci count.

2015A23.goal: $x^2-ax+2a$ has integer roots; we sum all possible $a$. Vieta gives two equations in the roots; eliminating $a$ leaves a factorable equation.
2015A23.approach: Eliminate $a$: $rs=2(r+s)$, which factors as $(r-2)(s-2)=4$. List integer factor pairs of $4$ (including negatives), find $(r,s)$, then $a=r+s$, and add distinct values.
2015A23.bridge: Use Vieta to get $(r-2)(s-2)=4$ and list factor pairs.
2015A23.shortcut: Don't forget negative factor pairs of $4$.
2015A23.recognize: Integer roots with a parameter: Vieta plus Simon's trick to factor.

2015A24.goal: A quadrilateral with right angles at $B$ and $C$, $AB=2$, and $CD=AD$ has integer sides and perimeter $p<2015$. We count possible $p$. Drop a perpendicular to turn $CD=AD$ into a Pythagorean condition.

tools.name: Right trapezoid
tools.why: Drop a perpendicular from $A$ to $CD$; the horizontal leg is $BC$ and the vertical leg is $CD-2$.

2015A24.approach: Let $BC=x$, $CD=AD=y$. Pythagoras gives $x^2+(y-2)^2=y^2$, i.e. $x^2=4y-4$. So $x=2m$ and $y=m^2+1$. Write $p$ in terms of $m$ and count $m$.

steps.title: Pythagoras
steps.explain: $x^2+(y-2)^2=y^2$ gives $x^2=4y-4$. So $x=2m$ and $y=m^2+1$ for a positive integer $m$.

2015A24.bridge: Use Pythagoras to get $x=2m$, $y=m^2+1$, then bound $p$.
2015A24.shortcut: Each $m$ gives a distinct $p$ since $p$ increases with $m$.
2015A24.recognize: Right trapezoids with a slanted side equal to a base: drop a perpendicular and use Pythagoras; parity often forces a parametrisation.

2015A25.goal: Two random points on the boundary of a unit square; we want $P(\text{distance}\ge\tfrac12)$. By symmetry, put the first point on the bottom side and case on which side the second lands.

tools.name: Symmetry
tools.fact: \text{First point on the bottom side, }(x,0),\ x\sim U[0,1]

tools.name: Probability as area
tools.fact: P=\text{area in the unit square of parameters}
tools.why: Two uniform parameters on a side give a uniform point in $[0,1]^2$.

tools.name: Quarter disc
tools.why: A quarter of a disc of radius $\tfrac12$.

2015A25.approach: Second point on the same side, the opposite side, or one of the two adjacent sides (each probability $\tfrac14$). Compute the conditional probability in each case and average.

steps.title: Opposite and adjacent sides
steps.explain: Opposite side: distance $\ge1$, probability $1$. Adjacent side, e.g. $(0,v)$: distance$^2=x^2+v^2$; it is less than $\tfrac14$ on a quarter disc of area $\tfrac\pi{16}$, so probability $1-\tfrac\pi{16}$.

check.q: What is the area of a quarter disc of radius $\tfrac12$?

2015A25.bridge: Fix the first point on one side and average over the four sides for the second.
solution: Put the first point on the bottom side.
Same side: $\tfrac14$. Opposite: $1$. Each adjacent side: $1-\tfrac{\pi}{16}$.
2015A25.shortcut: Only the adjacent-side case involves $\pi$; the rest are simple.
traps: Forgetting the factor $2$ for two adjacent sides.
Using a full disc instead of a quarter.
2015A25.recognize: Random points on a polygon's boundary: fix one side by symmetry and case on the other point's side; each case is an area problem.
